\section{Evidence hierarchy and provenance}
\label{sec:S0}

The paper labels the epistemic status of every block explicitly; the confirmatory replications are \emph{internal} replications (same datasets, corrected instrument, fresh seeds), not external validations. The registered core, ownership and size controls, policy comparison, feasibility instruments, chronological boundary and exploratory discovery remain distinct. The source-row-disjoint full-drift size and common-harness blocks use seeds 6001--6030 and 5001--5030. Their governing integrity sensitivity assigns exact cleaned raw feature groups wholly to roles and repeats the same central questions on virgin seeds 7001--7030 (B2) and 8001--8030 (B1); it is the last authorized scientific block and narrows, rather than erases, the historical findings. Where the sensitivity addresses a current claim, its interpretation governs.
The chronological tier supplies external empirical support on thirteen enumerated streams and limits the scope of generalization; it neither estimates nor bounds deployment harm frequency.

\section{The initial exploratory study (harness v1)}

\subsection{Updating is regime-dependent and sometimes harmful (initial study)}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{docs/img/fig1_regime_spectrum.pdf}
\caption{Readaptation value is regime-dependent and sometimes harmful: best detector-triggered gain over no-adaptation per dataset and attack regime.}
\label{fig:1}
\end{figure}
\input{tables/table1_regime_taxonomy.tex}
Under progressive drift, an unadapted classifier degrades and triggered readaptation can recover much of the loss --- on CICIDS2017. Averaged over 30 seeds and 100 post-drift windows, the best detector-triggered strategy recovers +19.5 balanced-accuracy (BA) points over no-adaptation in the Friday-DDoS regime, +11.9 in Wednesday, +7.6 in WebAttacks and +6.2 in PortScan (Table~\ref{tab:table1_regime_taxonomy}, Fig.~\ref{fig:1}). This is the familiar picture that motivates adaptive NIDS. (The per-regime \emph{best} detector is descriptive, not a tuned choice: with a single pre-specified detector, KS-max, the taxonomy is unchanged --- +5.5 to +18.6 BA points across the four CICIDS regimes, +1.5 and +0.2 on UNSW-NB15, $-$2.4 on ToN-IoT.)


The picture does not survive to independent data. On UNSW-NB15 the best recovery is marginal (+1.4 points for DoS, +0.5 for Reconnaissance), and on ToN-IoT Scanning it becomes \emph{negative} for the SVC-RBF downstream used here: no detector-triggered strategy matches a no-adaptation baseline (best adaptive $-$0.5 points; worst $-$4.6), so the correct decision there is \textbf{not to adapt} (Fig.~\ref{fig:1}). This net-harm is downstream-dependent --- it does not appear for more robust classifiers --- while the degradation regularity that tracks it is not (Supplementary \S S1.6). The effect is not a balanced-accuracy artifact: under attack-F1 the CICIDS benefits grow (e.g. +32.3 F1 points for DDoS) and ToN-IoT remains harmful for every detector (Energy $-$0.2, KS-max $-$4.6 F1 points). We stress the claim is not "adaptation usually hurts" --- it is that the \emph{sign} of the payoff is regime- and dataset-dependent, spanning +19.5 to $-$4.6 BA points, which is precisely what an adaptive system must anticipate.


% (fig:9 kept in the main body)
Why does adaptation help enormously in one regime and hurt in another? In the evaluated fixed-generator settings the state of the deployed model was consistently more predictive than the amount of drift, and we establish that with two facts --- stated carefully, because the naive statistic invites a coupling objection. First, \textbf{retraining restores accuracy to a nearly regime-invariant level}: across the seven SVC-RBF regimes, post-adaptation BA varies far less than the deployed-model BA it replaces ($\sigma$ = 3.5 vs.\ 7.4 points; regressing the gain on deployed BA gives slope $-$0.87). Under a fixed candidate generator, the benefit of adapting is therefore largely the deployed model's \emph{headroom} to that restored level: r = $-$0.89 between deployed-model BA and gain (descriptive scatter in Fig.~\ref{fig:2}), r = $-$0.81 (bootstrap CI95 [$-$0.94, $-$0.59], 16 model$\times$regime points) pooled across all four downstream classifiers (Fig.~\ref{fig:2b}). We deliberately do not rest the argument on the correlation coefficient itself: since the gain subtracts deployed BA, r is mathematically coupled to it, and an exhaustive re-pairing null holding both observed marginals yields a median r of $-$0.91 --- the observed value is no more extreme (p = 0.80; Table~\ref{tab:table7_mechanism_law_robustness}). The substance is the compression of the restored level, not the coefficient --- and the evidence we treat as central is the \emph{per-trigger} version of this fact, which shares no algebraic term between predictor and outcome: at individual triggered decisions under the hardened harness, the incumbent's degradation over the five preceding windows predicts the candidate-minus-incumbent value over the five following windows, while the detector's score at the same decisions shows no consistent association (per-trigger figure, clustered CIs and hierarchical model in \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper). Second, and free of any coupling, \textbf{the detector's own score carries almost no information about that headroom within a deployment}: over the 30 streams of each regime, the correlation between a detector's score and the gain from its own triggered adaptations has median +0.06 (maximum 0.13) across regimes, whereas deployed-model BA tracks the gain within every regime (median $-$0.68). Across regimes, classical detector scores do co-vary with the benefit (r = 0.75--0.94) --- larger drifts both fire detectors and degrade models --- but that cross-regime association is unavailable to a deployed detector calibrated on its own reference, and the persistence policies built on those scores fail to prevent harm (\S S1.3). The regularity itself is robust to disaggregation: at individual-stream level r = $-$0.91 (210 regime$\times$seed points), stable under seed resampling (CI95 [$-$0.90, $-$0.88]) and under removing any one regime (r between $-$0.72 and $-$0.92) or dataset --- with the expected range-restriction attenuation, not inversion, when all four CICIDS benefit regimes are removed at once (r = $-$0.52; Table~\ref{tab:table7_mechanism_law_robustness}). Where the deployed model has already collapsed (DDoS: 69.8\% without adaptation), retraining on a fresh window is a large gain; where it remains strong (ToN-IoT: 92.2\%), replacing a well-generalized model with a narrowly-fit current-window model is a net loss.


This exposes the core problem. Drift detectors answer \emph{"has the distribution changed?"}, but an adaptive NIDS needs \emph{"will retraining improve the classifier?"} --- and these are different questions. We quantify the gap with the per-stream policy oracle of \S\ref{sec:outcomes} of the main paper (holding the detector fixed); being a policy-selection bound, it understates the headroom of perfect per-trigger decisions. The resulting \emph{regret} of naive triggering is essentially zero where adaptation always helps (Wednesday, DDoS: 0.00 points, adaptation hurt on 0\% of streams) and largest where it hurts (ToN-IoT: 3.53 points for QK-ZZ, CI95 [1.76, 5.54], adaptation hurt on 67\% of streams), scaling monotonically with harm frequency (Table~\ref{tab:table4_oracle_regret}, Fig.~\ref{fig:3}). The headroom left by naive triggering is real and concentrated exactly where the deployed model is already good.


\subsection{Detector sensitivity does not resolve the decision}

\input{tables/table2_phase2_gate_summary.tex}
Because drift detectors are blind to model degradation, improving the detector cannot solve the problem --- and it does not. Quantum-kernel MMD monitors do define distinct \emph{operating points} on CICIDS2017 (QK-MMD ZZ triggers 1.8--2.1 fewer readaptations than Energy distance at equivalent accuracy in Wednesday/DDoS, and inverts in PortScan), but at a ~114$\times$ monitoring-runtime cost, and these profiles do not replicate externally. Critically, the regime taxonomy and the harmful-adaptation outcome are identical for classical and quantum detectors (Fig.~\ref{fig:3}, Tables~\ref{tab:table1_regime_taxonomy} and~\ref{tab:table2_phase2_gate_summary}): on ToN-IoT, naive triggering is net-harmful whether the trigger is KS-max ($-$1.4 points) or QK-ZZ ($-$3.7 points; Table~\ref{tab:table2_phase2_gate_summary}). Among the monitors evaluated, the operative lever is the adapt/no-adapt decision, not the similarity measure that fires the trigger.


\subsection{Simple confirmation and cooldown policies do not prevent harm}


If the decision is the lever, the natural fix is a smarter trigger policy. We pre-specified a grid of alarm-confirmation (k-of-n) and cooldown policies and evaluated them against fixed success criteria (preserve benefit in PortScan; avoid harm in ToN-IoT; do not degrade UNSW). None passed: in the harmful regime the tested policies remained far below no-adaptation and did not reduce adaptations relative to a conservative legacy baseline (Table~\ref{tab:table5_phase1_negative}). Confirmation and cooldown act on the \emph{persistence} of distributional change --- a signal that, within the evaluated triggered decisions, carried no consistent information about whether adaptation helps. This negative result motivates a policy that acts on the right quantity.


\subsection{A label-efficient validate-before-commit gate: the initial-study result}


\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{docs/img/fig4_phase2_gate.pdf}
\caption{The validate-before-commit gate preserves benefit and avoids harm at these evaluated operating points, with the same sign pattern for a classical (KS-max) and a quantum (QK-ZZ) detector (policies also differ by hatch; magnitudes differ; see text).}
\label{fig:4}
\end{figure}
We introduce a decision gate that acts directly on estimated model improvement. On each drift trigger, a candidate model is retrained as usual, but it is \textbf{deployed only if it beats the incumbent on a small labeled probe} drawn from the current window (budget 32 or 64 flows); otherwise the incumbent is kept. We evaluate the gate against the same pre-specified criteria (30 seeds, 100 windows, legacy trigger fixed so the gate is the only designed difference) across the benefit (PortScan), mixed (UNSW Reconnaissance) and harmful (ToN-IoT) regimes, for both a classical (KS-max) and a quantum (QK-ZZ) detector (Table~\ref{tab:table2_phase2_gate_summary}, Fig.~\ref{fig:4}).

\input{tables/table3_phase2_paired_ci.tex}
The gate passes every criterion for both detectors. In the harmful regime it turns net-harmful naive triggering into net benefit: ToN-IoT gain moves from $-$1.36 (KS-max) and $-$3.69 (QK-ZZ) points to +0.93 and +1.06, \textbf{significantly above naive triggering} (+2.30 points, CI95 [1.15, 3.63] for KS-max; +4.74, [2.47, 7.69] for QK-ZZ; Table~\ref{tab:table3_phase2_paired_ci}) and, notably, \textbf{significantly above no-adaptation itself} (+0.93, [0.53, 1.36]; +1.06, [0.77, 1.40]) --- the gate does not merely stop adapting, it commits the minority of beneficial adaptations while rejecting the harmful majority. In the benefit regime it preserves the full gain (PortScan +8.3/+8.4 points, statistically indistinguishable from naive; formally, benefit preservation was pre-specified as \emph{non-inferiority} at a 0.3-point margin, and the paired gate$-$naive CI95 lower bounds --- $\ge$ $-$0.12 across both detectors and both budgets --- clear it), and it does not degrade the mixed regime. The label cost is small: roughly 100--160 labeled flows over a 100-window stream at budget 32.


The gate's power comes from labels, not from the confirmation heuristic: a zero-label variant that commits on deployed-vs-candidate prediction \emph{disagreement} fails, remaining significantly below no-adaptation in the harmful regime ($-$4.95 and $-$5.26 points; Table~\ref{tab:table2_phase2_gate_summary}). A handful of target-labeled flows per confirmed drift therefore converts net-harmful naive updating into net benefit across the evaluated benefit, marginal and harm regimes --- without giving up the benefit, and matching what \S S1.5 shows even state-of-the-art label-free estimators do not. We are precise about ``safe'': the point rule is not a formal guarantee (\S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper reports its residual harmful-commit rate, 15--32\% of commits, and the risk-controlled gates that bound it); the claim here is average harm-avoidance at this operating point, not a certified safety property. Because the gate behaves the same way (same sign pattern) for the classical and quantum detectors (Fig.~\ref{fig:4}), the contribution is a detector-agnostic decision mechanism.


\subsection{Gate robustness (post-registration)}


\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{docs/img/fig5_label_budget_curve.pdf}
\caption{Label-efficiency frontier: gain over no-adaptation versus probe budget; regimes differ by marker and line style as well as colour.}
\label{fig:5}
\end{figure}
Ten extensions beyond the pre-specified design (explicitly labeled as robustness, not part of the confirmatory claim) probe the gate's limits. \emph{Label efficiency:} sweeping the probe budget from 8 to 128 flows (KS-max, 30 seeds; Fig.~\ref{fig:5}) shows the gate is remarkably label-cheap --- in this initial study even the smallest budget avoided harm, ~8 labeled flows per confirmed drift ($\approx$23 per stream) lifting ToN-IoT gain from $-$1.36 (naive) to +0.38, plateauing near +1.1 by budget 32--64 (the hardened-harness re-run sharpens this: at $b{=}8$ harm is reduced but not converted to net benefit, fixing the operating point at $b{=}32$; \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper); benefit-regime gain is flat at every budget. A few dozen labels, not hundreds, suffice in this balanced-probe setting. \emph{Benefit breadth:} beyond PortScan the gate preserves --- and slightly improves --- the benefit in the two strongest benefit regimes, Wednesday (naive +15.39 $\to$ +16.32) and DDoS (naive +24.81 $\to$ +25.27), preserving benefit in all three benefit regimes tested --- the exception being the deep-benefit chronological replays, where a stale probe imposes a measured, metric-dependent premium (\S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper).


\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{docs/img/fig8_probe_poison.pdf}
\caption{The gate remains harm-avoiding under randomly corrupted validation labels (up to 40\% flipped, initial study; replicated on the hardened harness in \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper).}
\label{fig:8}
\end{figure}
\emph{Label latency:} the probe need not be current. Drawing it from traffic labeled up to 20 windows in the past (Fig.~\ref{fig:7}) leaves the gate safe and effective at every lag --- in the harmful regime the gate holds at +0.9 to +1.1 (vs naive $-$1.36) for lags of 5, 10 and 20 windows, and the benefit regimes are essentially unchanged --- so the method tolerates realistic labeling delay rather than requiring instantaneous labels. \emph{Harm breadth:} the net-harm of naive triggering (with the fragile SVC-RBF downstream) is not confined to one ToN-IoT regime --- it also appears in ToN-IoT DDoS (naive \textbf{$-$16.81}) and Injection ($-$1.21), and the gate converts all three to net-positive (+1.26, +0.80, +0.93). \emph{Cost knob:} raising the commit margin $\varepsilon$ from 0 to 0.01--0.02 cuts committed adaptations by ~30\% (e.g. PortScan 3.1$\to$2.2 commits) at equal downstream gain, giving a simple operating characteristic that trades update frequency for benefit. \emph{Randomly corrupted validation labels:} because the gate trusts a labeled probe, we test a faulty labeler (or non-adaptive attacker) that flips a uniformly random fraction of the probe labels --- the random variant of the label-flipping poisoning threat against SVM-family learners \cite{biggio2012poisoning} (Fig.~\ref{fig:8}). The gate avoids harm under this corruption process: even with 40\% of validation labels corrupted --- near the point where the probe is pure noise --- it still matches-or-beats naive triggering in every regime (ToN-IoT degrades gracefully from +0.93 to +0.32 but never goes negative; benefit and mixed regimes are essentially unchanged). Label noise perturbs the deployed and candidate estimates symmetrically, so it moves the gate along the naive-to-oracle line without pushing it below the safe baseline. (A candidate-aware adversary that chooses \emph{which} labels to flip is a strictly stronger threat we do not model; \S7 of the main paper.) \emph{Label-free estimators head-to-head:} the zero-label variant of \S S1.4 is deliberately naive, so we also instantiate the two standard label-free accuracy estimators --- ATC \cite{garg2022atc} and DoC \cite{guillory2021doc} --- as gates in the same harness: each model estimates its target-window accuracy from its own confidences plus a labeled validation sample drawn at its training time, using zero target-window labels. Both avoid harm --- on the fragile SVC-RBF downstream, ToN-IoT moves from $-$1.36 (naive) to +0.40 (ATC) and +1.16 (DoC) --- but both pay for safety with benefit: on PortScan they lose 24\% (ATC) and 60\% (DoC) of the naive gain ($-$1.86 [$-$3.48, $-$0.17] and $-$4.64 [$-$6.86, $-$2.26] vs naive, CI95), and they remain significantly below naive even for random forest with native predicted probabilities. Among the evaluated gates none dominates: DoC reaches the higher harm-regime point estimate ($+1.16$ vs the probe's $+0.93$ in this study) while surrendering most of the benefit-regime gain, so the labeled probe's distinctive property is that it alone preserves the full benefit-regime gain while converting the harm regime. The mechanism mirrors the degradation law: confidence-based estimates are trustworthy only while the incumbent is healthy --- exactly the regime where the gate is least needed --- and misrank incumbent against candidate once the incumbent has degraded, which is where the benefit lives; related estimators share the same calibration premise \cite{jiang2022disagreement,baek2022agreement,rosenfeld2023dis2,deng2021labels}. \emph{Replay retraining:} the harmful baseline retrains on a narrow current window and fully replaces the incumbent, so we also test the standard label-free mitigation --- retrain-current-plus-replay, augmenting each candidate's training set with an equal-size sample from the reference regime (50/50) --- under pre-fixed criteria (KS-max, SVC-RBF, 30 seeds). The tested fixed 50/50 replay does not rescue naive triggering: in the harm regime it remains significantly net-harmful ($-$4.54, CI95 [$-$7.06, $-$2.34] vs no-adaptation; worse than full replacement's $-$1.36, since under a still-advancing ramp a replay-anchored candidate misfits later windows even more), and in the benefit regime it \emph{loses} part of the gain (+6.59 vs +7.79 naive). The gate, by contrast, is orthogonal to the update rule: placed on top of replay it restores safety and benefit in every regime --- ToN-IoT +0.59, significantly above both no-adaptation ([0.23, 0.97]) and replay-naive (+5.13 [2.96, 7.60]); PortScan +8.26, recovering the benefit replay-naive loses (+1.66 [0.52, 3.04]). Harmful adaptation is therefore not an artifact of full-replacement retraining, and the gate's value composes with the update strategy. \emph{Probe prevalence:} the probes above are class-balanced, which presumes an enrichment mechanism. An initial low-prevalence experiment (conditioned on the probe containing at least one attack) suggested the gate was indifferent down to $\pi=0.01$; that conditioning turned out to force a minority-class flow into every probe and the claim was an artifact. \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper reports the corrected experiment, in which the attack count is drawn honestly as $\mathrm{Binomial}(b,\pi)$: the gate tolerates genuinely random inspection down to $\pi\approx0.05$, but its harm-regime guarantee dissolves at $\pi=0.01$ (where two-thirds of 32-flow probes contain no attack at all). We report the corrected bound and withdraw the stronger one. \emph{Candidate size and dimensionality:} two controls address the concern that the harm is a pipeline artifact. Size-matching \emph{under this study's frozen transformer and advancing full-drift ramp}: training every candidate on 2{,}000 flows per class --- the same budget as the initial model, removing the 4$\times$ size asymmetry --- \emph{deepens} the harm (ToN-IoT naive $-$5.34, CI95 [$-$8.73, $-$2.49], vs $-$1.36 at 512/class): a larger candidate fits the current mixture better and mis-specializes harder while the ramp keeps advancing, the opposite of what a small-sample explanation predicts in that configuration (the preregistered own-transformer zero-drift control of \S\ref{sec:sizematched} of the main paper and \S S8 finds that, with self-contained preprocessing and no drift, the mean effects are compatible with the registered $\pm0.5$-point margin (PortScan boundary-close; no absence claim) --- the two settings answer different questions and both are reported); the gate remains safe and beneficial throughout (+0.58 / +9.33 / +3.37 across the three regimes), and candidate size does shift the marginal regime's magnitude (UNSW +3.31 vs +0.92), so magnitudes are pipeline-dependent even where signs are not. Dimensionality: with the PCA bottleneck removed (full feature space, classical detector), the benefit grows (PortScan +16.2) and the harm regime's point estimate remains negative ($-$0.65 [$-$3.03, +1.44], not significant at 30 seeds) --- neither the candidate's sample size nor the 8-dimensional projection generates the phenomenon, though full dimensionality attenuates the harm and we report that plainly. \emph{Significance of the safety claim.} Paired bootstrap CIs in the harm regime confirm the guarantee is not noise: the gate significantly outperforms naive triggering under every label-latency and every probe-poison level tested (CI95 excludes zero), and in no robustness condition --- across downstream models, latencies or poison levels --- is it significantly \emph{worse} than either naive triggering or no-adaptation. For the robust downstream models where the gate is not significantly better than naive, the comparison resolves no difference; failure to reject equality is not a non-inferiority result and does not establish that the gate is never worse.


\subsection{Generalization across downstream classifiers}


\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{docs/img/fig6_downstream_generalization.pdf}
\caption{Generalization across four downstream classifiers: net-harm is specific to SVC-RBF in this study; naive and gate policies differ by hatch as well as colour.}
\label{fig:6}
\end{figure}
\input{tables/table6_downstream_generalization.tex}
To test whether the phenomenon and the solution depend on the downstream model, we repeat the three regimes with the KS-max trigger for four downstream classifiers --- SVC-RBF, random forest, logistic regression and MLP (20 seeds; Table~\ref{tab:table6_downstream_generalization}, Fig.~\ref{fig:6}). Three findings stand out, and we report them plainly because they refine the headline.


First, \textbf{the degradation--headroom regularity generalizes.} Across all four classifiers the benefit of adaptation tracks deployed-model degradation: where the frozen model is weak the gain is large (e.g. random forest and MLP on PortScan start at 69--70\% no-adaptation BA and gain +27 points; logistic regression on ToN-IoT starts at 84\% and gains +6.7), and where the frozen model is already strong the gain is small (random forest on ToN-IoT starts at 97\% and gains only +1.9). Pooled across all four classifiers the degradation--benefit correlation remains strong (r = $-$0.81, \S S1.1; Fig.~\ref{fig:2b}): the relationship is a property of the adaptation problem, not of SVC.


Second, \textbf{whether the effect crosses into net harm is downstream-specific.} The negative-gain result --- naive triggering below no-adaptation --- occurs only for SVC-RBF on ToN-IoT ($-$1.36 points); random forest (+1.88), logistic regression (+6.70) and MLP (+0.24) all remain non-negative there (Fig.~\ref{fig:6}). SVC-RBF is fragile enough on this regime that retraining on a narrow current window loses more than it gains; more robust downstream models do not. We therefore do not claim that naive readaptation is universally harmful --- only that it can be, for fragile models, exactly where the regularity predicts the smallest headroom.


Third, and most important for deployment, \textbf{the gate avoids material harm in all twelve settings of this study.} Across all four downstream classifiers and all three regimes (twelve settings), the labeled-probe gate shows no material deficit against no-adaptation or naive triggering; the largest observed mean deficit vs.\ naive anywhere is 0.11 BA points (random forest on UNSW Reconnaissance), within seed noise (Table~\ref{tab:table6_downstream_generalization}). (The hardened-harness replication puts sharper bounds on this claim --- including one statistically resolvable but immaterial 0.01-point deficit, and a real chronological stream where the premium is material; \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper.) This empirical harm-avoidance pattern --- an observation of this exploratory study, not a certified property --- holds even in the settings where naive triggering is already fine (the gate simply commits), and rescues the one setting where it is harmful. The solution generalizes across downstream models even though the harm does not.


\subsection{Controls}


The findings are robust to the evaluation metric (the taxonomy and harmful-adaptation result hold under attack-F1; \S S1.1). Quantum monitors do not reduce nuisance triggers on benign drift (QK-MMD ZZ 1.40 vs Energy 1.03 false triggers), so their value cannot be framed as cleaner benign-drift filtering; and an expensive Random-Forest downstream shows that quantum monitoring runtime can dominate total operational cost. A pre-specified feature-map sensitivity study finds no deeper map that unlocks a stronger quantum advantage. (Full tables for both: reproducibility artifact \cite{fernandezbarrios2026artifact}.) These controls reinforce, rather than qualify, the central conclusion: distribution-shift magnitude alone is not a sufficient commit signal.




\section{Registered-extension details relocated from the main paper}
The subsections below are verbatim accounts of registered extensions whose conclusions are summarized in \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper; they are relocated here for compactness, not because their status is exploratory --- each was locked in a registered amendment note before its runs.

\subsection{Canonical performance-aware monitors: reference-implementation validation and budget sweep}

\textbf{Canonical monitors, validated against reference implementations.} Amendment 003 added the canonical performance-aware triggers (800 monitoring labels/stream): our batch DDM captures much of the benefit (PortScan +6.81) but is itself \textbf{net-harmful in the harm regime} ($-$2.59 [$-$5.90, $-$0.34]) --- monitoring the model's own error still commits harmful updates once a transient fires the trigger --- and the gate rescues it (+0.19). Because bespoke implementations invite doubt, amendment 004 cross-checks both monitors against the \texttt{river} reference implementations. Our DDM agrees with river's on synthetic Bernoulli step streams (94\% fire/no-fire agreement, comparable delays), and \emph{in-harness river-DDM replicates the key result}: fed the same 8 labels/window as individual outcomes, it remains net-harmful in ToN-IoT ($-$2.23 [$-$5.29, $-$0.05]) and benefit-lossy in UNSW (+0.14 vs naive +1.21). Our window-rate ADWIN variant, by contrast, proved insensitive (57\% agreement --- it under-fires), so we report the reference ADWIN instead: at these monitoring rates it never fires in two regimes and fires rarely in PortScan, forfeiting most of the benefit (+1.77 vs +8.25). The direction of the amendment-003 claim survives under reference implementations; the specific "never fires" wording was an artifact of our variant, and we correct it. Because a single budget invites the objection that the monitors were starved, a registered sweep raised the monitoring budget to 3{,}200 and 8{,}000 labels per stream (4$\times$ and 10$\times$): no budget fixes the pattern --- reference DDM stays net-harmful or useless in ToN-IoT ($-$1.04 [$-$1.87, $-$0.37] at 4$\times$; $-$0.45 at 10$\times$) and loses benefit elsewhere as its budget grows (PortScan +7.08 at 10$\times$ vs naive's +8.25), while reference ADWIN stays silent in ToN-IoT at every budget. The claim is therefore budget-conditional but robust across the two orders of magnitude evaluated: under these monitoring configurations, labels spent on the commit decision bought a better accuracy--cost trade-off than labels spent monitoring.

\subsection{The v1 robustness envelope on the hardened harness}

\textbf{The v1 robustness envelope, re-established (and partly corrected) on v2.} The initial study's three operational robustness claims were re-run on the hardened harness (descriptive, same pristine seeds, paired against the shared naive arm). \emph{Budget:} the gate's benefit is stable for $b \ge 32$ (ToN +0.79; $b{=}64$: +0.92; $b{=}128$: +1.01), but the initial study's ``8 labels suffice'' does \emph{not} fully replicate: at $b{=}8$ the gate still reduces harm (+1.22 [0.46, 2.15] above naive) yet is no longer net-positive against no-adaptation ($-$0.42 [$-$1.15, 0.23]), and $b{=}16$ is borderline (+0.29 [$-$0.27, 0.77]). We therefore revise the recommended operating point to $b{=}32$. \emph{Label latency:} at 20 windows of staleness the harm regime holds fully (+0.95 [0.76, 1.19]) and the benefit regimes pay only a small, real cost (PortScan $-$0.47 [$-$0.74, $-$0.22] vs fresh lp32). \emph{Random label corruption:} harm \emph{avoidance} survives 40\% flipped probe labels (still +1.60 [0.79, 2.55] above naive), but net benefit over no-adaptation survives only to 25\% (+0.57 [0.25, 0.85]; at 40\%: $-$0.04 [$-$0.62, 0.49]) --- the corrected, sharper version of the initial claim.

\subsection{Natural-prevalence probes and evaluation: corrections and a retraction}

\textbf{Honest natural-prevalence probes: a claim we retract.} The initial study reported that the probe ``need not be balanced'' and retained full safety and benefit even at $\pi{=}0.01$. That test drew the probe with a forced minority-class flow (\texttt{max(1,\,$\lfloor b\pi \rceil$)}), so it was really an \emph{attack-enriched} probe containing exactly one attack --- not random inspection at $\pi$. A registered rerun samples the attack count as $\mathrm{Binomial}(b, \pi)$, allowing zero-attack probes, and the picture changes. At $\pi{=}0.10$ (2--3\% of probes contain no attack) the gate is unaffected. At $\pi{=}0.05$ (15--23\% zero-attack) it still holds (ToN +0.91 [0.67, 1.17]), at a small real cost in the benefit regime ($-$0.44 [$-$0.79, $-$0.12] vs the balanced probe). At $\pi{=}0.01$, where \emph{two-thirds} of 32-flow probes contain no attack at all, the harm-regime guarantee dissolves: +0.21 [$-$1.39, 1.15] --- no longer resolvable from zero. The corrected claim is therefore narrower and, we think, more useful: the gate tolerates genuinely random inspection down to roughly $\pi \approx 0.05$; below that, an operator must \emph{enrich} the probe (alert-guided or active sampling, $\approx 1/\pi$ inspections to find one attack) or accept that the commit decision is being made on benign traffic alone.

Separately, on natural-prevalence \emph{evaluation} streams, the corrected experiment --- with the detector also \emph{calibrated} at operating prevalence --- is reported in \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper, where the binding constraint turns out to be the starved monitor, not the gate. An earlier variant that calibrated on balanced windows but evaluated on imbalanced streams overstated trigger rates and gains (ToN naive $-$2.63, gated +0.80, lower FPR and alert volume under the gate) and is retained as exploratory.

\subsection{The two-stage health reference, recalibrated}

\textbf{The two-stage health reference, recalibrated.} The review noted that the two-stage gate compared each incumbent's health against the \emph{initial} model's reference, which stops being meaningful after the first commit. Resetting the reference on every commit to the new incumbent's accuracy on the (already labeled) commit half leaves the conclusions unchanged (ToN +0.11 [$-$0.27, 0.45] vs +0.15 [$-$0.15, 0.46] static; PortScan +7.88 vs +7.87), so the reported savings are not an artifact of a stale reference --- but the corrected variant is the one we recommend.

\subsection{Cumulative-generator controls under zero drift}

\textbf{Cumulative controls (amendment 011): the harm is not an artifact of duplication or regularization.} Review asked whether the cumulative generator's harm is confounded by with-replacement duplication (its training set is only 76--83\% unique rows), by omitting the incumbent's initial training set, or by holding the SVC penalty $C$ fixed as $n$ grows. We ran all three registered controls under zero drift. \emph{Deduplicating} the training rows (100\% unique) does \emph{not} remove the harm --- it \emph{deepens} it (ToN $-$9.46 $\to$ $-$10.74, PortScan $-$7.04 $\to$ $-$11.36), because more distinct current-regime rows mis-specialize the replacement harder. \emph{$n$-scaling} $C$ with the corrected $C\propto 1/n$ rule (stronger regularization as the set grows) likewise leaves it --- indeed slightly deepens it (ToN $-$10.62, PortScan $-$9.82, vs $-$9.46 / $-$7.04 at fixed $C{=}1$). \emph{Adding the initial training set} attenuates but does not eliminate it (ToN $-$8.27, PortScan $-$5.14) and flips the marginal UNSW case positive ($-$0.07 $\to$ +0.53) --- an honest boundary: where the healthy incumbent had almost nothing to lose, re-anchoring the candidate to the original data recovers a small gain. None of the controls that a ``just use more data / de-duplicate / re-regularize'' reading would predict to help actually removes the harm (the $n$-scaled control uses the corrected $C\propto 1/n$ regularization --- \emph{stronger} as the set grows --- and the harm persists there too); so the effect is not duplication or under-regularization. The ownership A/B control (\S S2.12, Table~\ref{tab:ab_equivalence}) then identifies what it \emph{is}: not re-estimation variance but the incumbent's frozen, incumbent-fit transformer, which disadvantages any challenger that inherits it --- the harm vanishes under an independent transformer and reappears under an incumbent-fit one.

\subsection{Chronological replays: the full per-replay account}

\textbf{Chronologically ordered subsampled replays: the gate's honest boundary, measured properly.} A first Friday replay (seeds 134--163) contained two implementation flaws, caught in external review: a stride mismatch let candidates train on ${\sim}$28k rows the stream never presented as evaluation windows, and its summary averaged plain accuracy (single-class windows) with balanced accuracy. We corrected the runner, registered the correction (amendment 004), and re-ran on fresh seeds with two additional CICIDS streams; a further registered amendment (005) added an \emph{external} chronological stream --- the raw UNSW-NB15 captures, 2.54M flows sorted by flow start time, incumbent trained on the first 30\% of the timeline (temporal-streams table in the main paper). The corrected picture is stronger in both directions, and the fourth stream completes it. The phenomenon is real: Tuesday-trained CICIDS incumbents collapse on all three days (BA 53--72\%) and drift-triggered retraining recovers +13.6 to +27.6 points --- deep-benefit territory, confirming the recovery is not an artifact of the ramps. The gate's boundary is sharper than the flawed run suggested: on Friday the gate surrenders 6.3 of naive's 13.6 recovered BA points ($-$6.34 [$-$6.83, $-$5.90]) and on Thursday 5.0 of 22.7, while on Wednesday it pays nothing (+0.40 [0.09, 0.74]). \emph{And on the external stream the account's central prediction holds}: the UNSW incumbent stays healthy (82.3\% BA, no collapse; 163/200 two-class windows, ${\sim}$21 triggers/stream), updating helps moderately (+7.33 [6.80, 7.85]), and the gate pays \emph{no premium at all} (+0.16 [$-$0.31, 0.63] vs naive on BA; +0.21 on accuracy) --- the insurance is free precisely where the incumbent's health makes the commit decision genuinely uncertain, which is where the gate's value concentrates. A fifth registered replay attempted to engineer chronological harm --- train on Wednesday (DoS-rich) and replay Thursday (sparse WebAttacks $\to$ Infiltration), hoping for a healthy incumbent facing weak candidates --- but the Wednesday-trained model collapses on Thursday too (48.7\% BA), producing another deep-benefit stream (naive +33.66, gate +18.58; premium $-$15.08 on BA, $-$0.08 [$-$0.30, 0.15] on accuracy --- the same metric-dependent pattern, at its most extreme). A sixth registered replay (amendment 009) targeted the healthy-incumbent corner directly --- a purely \emph{intra-day} CICIDS stream (Tuesday, train on the first 30\% of the timeline, stream the rest) so the incumbent faces the same day it trained on --- but it collapses there too (no-adaptation BA 49.5\%, naive +43.8, gate premium $-$5.66 [$-$8.62, $-$3.85]), because Tuesday's brute-force phase switches attack sub-type over the day (the training window contains only FTP-Patator, the stream only SSH-Patator), so a new variant appears that the incumbent never saw: deep benefit again, not a healthy incumbent. \emph{Chronological net-harm is therefore unobserved across these six replays, and within this first set the only healthy-incumbent chronological stream is the external UNSW-NB15 timeline (the pre-enumerated matrix of \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper adds two more)}: every CICIDS incumbent collapses on a later window --- even within a single day --- which is exactly the deep-benefit corner where the account says the gate has least to offer. This is a real limit on external validity for the harm result, and \S7 of the main paper states it --- though the mild-drift prediction test in the main paper shows that the harm is not confined to one dataset once the incumbent is allowed to stay healthy.

\input{tables/table_temporal_streams.tex}

Across the complete thirteen-replay matrix, the absence of observed net harm is therefore an external-support and generalization boundary only; it supplies no estimate or bound on deployment harm frequency.

These replays are \emph{chronologically ordered subsampled replays}, not full-capture replays: each processes 200 windows of 256 flows, strided to span the day, so a fraction of the capture is evaluated. The ordering, the labels and the causal availability of every probe are real; the sampling density is not. The premium is \emph{metric-dependent}: on overall accuracy the gate \emph{beats} naive on the same streams (Friday +4.19 [3.85, 4.52]; Thursday +1.23) while losing balanced accuracy on attack-mixed windows. Our first diagnosis --- that the gate inherits the benign-dominated \emph{class composition} of a natural-composition probe --- was put to a registered causal test (amendment 005): a stratified probe (16 per class wherever the past window contains both classes) leaves the premium unchanged (stratified$-$plain: $-$0.05 [$-$0.49, 0.41] on Friday), so the composition account is \emph{not supported} where it is testable --- with the caveat that roughly two-thirds of past windows are single-class, where stratification cannot act. The surviving explanation is probe \emph{staleness}: on a stream whose regime changes within a few windows, a nine-window-old probe --- whatever its composition --- misranks candidates whose relative merits have already shifted, and it systematically misranks them on the minority class first (which is why balanced accuracy pays and overall accuracy does not). We report this as a hypothesis consistent with the data, not a demonstrated mechanism; on streams known to sit deep in the benefit regime, naive triggering is already adequate. This is the one registered check where the gate costs real benefit, reported as such.

\subsection{How the leakage-free observed-data arm was reached (three registered iterations)}

\textbf{Each iteration closed a flaw that external review or our own assertions surfaced},
and the harm-regime conclusion survived all of them. Two earlier ones preceded the three
listed below. Amendment 006's arm drew the candidate and probe causally but still
\emph{recalibrated} the detector after every commit from the pools at the true severity ---
and because the gate and the naive loop commit at different times, that oracle state
interacts with the policy instead of cancelling between arms; amendment 007 rebuilt the
post-commit reference from the last eight \emph{observed} windows and its threshold from the
preceding observed windows' scores. The same amendment closed a second flaw we had missed:
because pools are sampled with replacement, window-disjoint was not \emph{row}-disjoint, so
the probe now excludes by exact row identity every flow that also occurs in the candidate's
training windows (27--38 such rows per stream had been shared). (i) Amendment 011 removed the
with-replacement stream, cutting candidate-training/future-evaluation collisions from
387--1{,}319 per stream to ${\approx}0$; (ii) amendment 012 replaced the naive-loop fallback
at early no-probe triggers with \texttt{reject}, so no commit is ever made without a
validating probe; (iii) amendment 013 made the value-deduplication \emph{global} with an
abort-on-exhaustion assertion (collisions \emph{exactly} zero) and added a minimum-window
rule before the observed detector threshold is recomputed. The ToN-IoT gate$-$naive contrast
across the four versions was $+3.86$ (leaky) $\to$ $+2.95$ $\to$ $+3.24$ $\to$ $+5.57$
(final): the effect was never an artifact of the leakage, and tightening the pipeline
\emph{strengthened} rather than weakened it. CICIDS-PortScan moved the other way --- its
small benefit-regime premium was partly leakage and settles at $+0.41$ --- which is the
honest counterpart and the reason we report both. The superseded intermediate numbers are
preserved in the registered amendment notes in the artifact repository, not in the paper.

\subsection{The pooled EB-CS probe-budget sweep (superseded in scope by the budget frontier)}

Amendment 011 asked whether the pooled empirical-Bernstein gate's abstention at $b{=}64$ was
a property of the rule or of the budget, using a three-point sweep on the per-proposal gate.
Raising the probe to 128 and 256 flows lifts it monotonically: CICIDS-PortScan
$+5.17 \to +7.31 \to +8.07$ (approaching the fixed 32-probe point gate's $+8.70$), and the
small benefits it had missed become resolvable (UNSW-Recon $+0.00 \to +0.12 \to +0.78$;
ToN-IoT at full drift $+0.00 \to +0.01 \to +0.12$), at a proportional labeling cost of
63/124/239 labels per decision. The conclusion --- \emph{the binding constraint is the label
budget, not the decision rule} --- is the same one the far larger registered budget frontier
of \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper reaches for the \emph{lifetime-budgeted} policies, which is why
the main text now carries that experiment and this three-point sweep is retained here as its
antecedent.

\subsection{Superseded risk-gate implementations: the Robbins CS and the Bonferroni sequential probe}

Two risk-controlled rules preceded the empirical-Bernstein machinery the paper now recommends,
and both are dominated by it. We record them here so the frontier's endpoints are documented.

\textbf{Robbins normal-mixture confidence sequence.} Commits only when a normal-mixture lower
confidence sequence on the per-flow correctness difference exceeds zero, bounding the
per-proposal probability of falsely establishing positive expected paired correctness on the
probe distribution by $\alpha$, uniformly over the inspection schedule (\S\ref{sec:riskgates} of the main
paper states the guarantee and its scope). Because the bound must budget for the worst-case
sub-Gaussian variance ($\sigma^2 \le 1$) rather than the observed one, at probe budgets
$\le 64$ flows it essentially never commits (gain $+0.00$ across all mild- and zero-drift
regimes). That is correct behaviour where there is no headroom, and it is the
maximally risk-averse endpoint of the point/LCB/McNemar/sequential frontier --- but it forgoes
benefit wherever headroom exists, which is exactly what the empirical-Bernstein sequence
recovers by using the empirical variance of a mostly-tied difference sequence.

\textbf{Bonferroni sequential probe.} Draws 16 flows, decides as soon as the evidence resolves
the sign, and buys more (to 64) only while the decision is in doubt, spending $\alpha/K$ at
each of $K{=}4$ looks so that stopping is valid. (A first heuristic version inspected a
fixed-sample interval at each look, which inflates the error rate under optional stopping;
external review noted this and the registered rule replaced it.) It spends 58--61 labels per
decision and is deliberately conservative: CICIDS-PortScan $+8.04$, i.e.\ $-1.08$
[$-1.38$, $-0.79$] below the fixed 32-label probe; UNSW-Recon $+1.00$; ToN-IoT $+0.16$. It is
also the rule that recovers essentially all of the zero-drift loss by refusing to commit
without evidence. The confidence sequences of \S3.5 subsume it: they are valid at every sample
size rather than at four pre-declared looks, and the empirical-Bernstein version is
strictly tighter at the same $\alpha$.

\subsection{Decision-quality of the lp32 gate on the logged triggers (relocated from main \S5.7)}

Using the logged five-window lookahead as ground truth (never available to the policy), the
lp32 gate's per-trigger operating point is: in the harm regime, rejection is almost always
right (95\% of rejections blocked a non-beneficial update; recall of beneficial updates 0.95)
and the gate cuts \emph{local per-decision regret} --- commit vs.\ reject on the gate policy's
own trigger states, against an always-commit rule on those identical states --- from 0.0452
to 0.0020, ${\sim}22\times$; in the benefit regime it still reduces this regret five-fold
(0.0028 vs 0.0140). Pooled across 308 triggers: precision 0.74, recall 0.87, regret 0.0030
vs 0.0212; horizon reruns at 1/3/5/10 leave the reductions essentially unchanged, and the
marginal regime is honestly a wash at every horizon. The gate does commit some harmful
updates (23\% of its commits have negative realized value, mostly small) --- it is a cheap
statistical filter, not an oracle.

\subsection{VBC-SG: continuation modes, risk budget and stated properties (relocated from main \S3.5)}
\label{sec:S2_vbcsg}

The main text (\S3.5) states the risk-controlled gates at the level needed to read the results.
This subsection carries the implementation-level definitions that were previously in the main
text; nothing here changes the guarantee or its scope.

\textbf{Levels and stratification.} The confidence sequences run at $\alpha=0.10$; the
exact-McNemar gate at its registered $\alpha=0.05$ (stricter, hence if anything \emph{more}
conservative at zero drift); re-running McNemar at $\alpha=0.10$ leaves the zero-drift conclusion
unchanged ($\approx 0$ commits; main \S5.7). The effective per-arm $\alpha$ is recorded in the run
manifest. Because the probe is drawn with \emph{fixed class quotas} ($b/2$ per class) rather than
i.i.d.\ from one distribution, the pooled tests match the sampling only approximately; the
\emph{stratified} variants close that gap by lower-bounding each class's mean correctness
difference at $\alpha/2$ (Bonferroni over the two classes) and committing iff
$\tfrac12(L_{\mathrm{ben}}+L_{\mathrm{att}})>0$, which bounds the false-superiority probability for
the \emph{balanced-accuracy} difference under the stratified design actually used. We evaluate a
\emph{fixed-sample} version (per-class one-sided normal LCB; no sequential validity) and the
\emph{anytime-valid} version, in which each class's bound is an empirical-Bernstein confidence
sequence inspected at the same sequential looks as the pooled gate; only the latter supports the
anytime-valid claim.

\textbf{The family and its named member.} The rules of main \S3.5 form a family --- a sequential
decision-support instantiation for settings in which validation is chosen --- and what the paper
contributes is that family together with the frontier it spans, \emph{not} a claim that any one
member dominates, not a claim of fundamental mathematical novelty, and not the source of the
paper's final verdict. We name its maximally-guaranteed member, the \emph{Validate-Before-Commit
Sequential Gate}, because it is the configuration that carries every layer of control at once;
main \S5.7 shows what each layer costs, and that a \emph{less} stratified sibling and even the
no-additional-label strict rule are the better buy at some operating points.

\textbf{Continuation modes under deferral.} Deferral raises a question the gate must answer
explicitly: once the stream drifts \emph{between} windows, what does a sequence that keeps
acquiring labels at later windows estimate? Three registered continuation modes make the answer
precise. \emph{Cohort-sim} (fixed-target): additional labels are resampled from the proposal-time
target distribution available to the simulator (the mixture the proposal was raised on), so the
sequence estimates one fixed mean and the per-proposal guarantee is the clean fixed-target one.
Cohort-sim does not model retention and delayed adjudication of a literal production cohort, so
this acquisition scheme is not claimed to be directly deployable. \emph{Refresh}: each deferral
window opens a \emph{fresh} evidence set tested at $\alpha_j/(1+D)$ (Bonferroni over the at most
$1+D$ sets a proposal with deferral cap $D$ may open), so observations from temporally different
targets are never mixed. \emph{Accumulate} (retained as an ablation): the same sequences continue
on labels drawn at each current window; by Proposition~1 of the main paper (proof in \S S4) this
mode still bounds false commits, but only under the \emph{weak conditional null} that the
challenger is at no time conditionally better on the probe stream, which is why cohort and
refresh are the interpretable variants under drift.

\textbf{Deployment-long risk budget.} A deployment-long risk budget allocates each proposal's
level $\alpha_j$ by a declared spending schedule (Bonferroni $\alpha_{\mathrm{life}}/M$, or the
$p$-series $\alpha_j = 6\alpha_{\mathrm{life}}/(\pi^2 j^2)$, which needs no horizon $M$); the
effective $\alpha_j$ of every proposal is logged. Without a spending schedule the guarantee is
\emph{per proposal} only (union bound $M\alpha$ over $M$ tested proposals); a lifetime bound
requires alpha-spending across proposals or a single deployment-long e-process, which is exactly
what the risk budget supplies.

\textbf{Four properties, stated at the strength we can support.} (i) \emph{Per-proposal}: the
probability of falsely establishing positive expected balanced-accuracy difference on the probe
distribution is at most $\alpha_j$, uniformly over the sampling schedule --- under within-class
i.i.d.\ sampling from the proposal's target for the cohort/refresh modes, and under the weak
conditional null of Proposition~1 for the accumulate mode. (ii) \emph{Deployment-long}: by the
union bound over the spending schedule, the probability of \emph{ever} making such a false commit
over the deployment is at most $\alpha_{\mathrm{life}}$, under the same assumptions. (iii)
\emph{Label cost}: labels per proposal are bounded by the per-window budget times $(1 + D)$, and
the observed cost concentrates far below the bound because most proposals resolve early. (iv)
\emph{Transfer}: none of (i)--(iii) bounds future deployed accuracy unless the probe is
representative of the evaluation horizon --- the stale-probe and dependence results (main
\S5.4--\S5.5) quantify exactly where that premise fails. No stronger guarantee is claimed; the
empirical sections of the main paper report the price of each.

\section{Proof of Proposition 1 (conditional validity of the commit e-process)}
\label{sec:s4proof}

\noindent\textbf{Setting.} Per class, the gate observes per-flow correctness differences
$d_1, d_2, \dots \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$ in adjudication order, mapped to $x_i = (d_i+1)/2 \in [0,1]$.
The implementation maintains, before observing $x_i$, the predictable plug-ins
$\hat\mu_{i-1} = (1/2 + \sum_{j<i} x_j)/i$ and
$\hat\sigma^2_{i-1} = (1/4 + \sum_{j<i} (x_j - \hat\mu_{j-1})^2)/i$, and the predictable betting
fraction $\lambda_i = \min\{3/4,\ \sqrt{2\log(1/\alpha) / (\hat\sigma^2_{i-1}\, i \log(i+1))}\}$.
With $\psi_E(\lambda) = -\log(1-\lambda) - \lambda$, define the wealth process
$$W_n \;=\; \exp\Big(\sum_{i\le n} \lambda_i \big(x_i - \tfrac12\big) \;-\; \sum_{i\le n} \psi_E(\lambda_i)\,\big(x_i - \hat\mu_{i-1}\big)^2\Big), \qquad W_0 = 1 .$$
The gate's commit condition --- the empirical-Bernstein lower bound on $\mathbb{E}[d]$
exceeding $0$, i.e.\ the lower bound on $\mathbb{E}[x]$ exceeding $1/2$ --- rearranges exactly to
$\sum_i \lambda_i (x_i - \tfrac12) - \sum_i \psi_E(\lambda_i)(x_i - \hat\mu_{i-1})^2 > \log(1/\alpha)$,
i.e.\ the event $\{W_n > 1/\alpha\}$: the confidence-sequence inversion and the e-process
threshold are the same object.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Claim.} If $\mathbb{E}[x_i \mid \mathcal F_{i-1}] \le 1/2$ for every $i$ (the weak
null: the challenger is at no time conditionally better), with no stationarity or identical-distribution
assumption, then $(W_n)$ is a nonnegative supermartingale and
$\Pr(\exists n : W_n > 1/\alpha) \le \alpha$.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Proof.} Write $\mu_i = \mathbb{E}[x_i \mid \mathcal F_{i-1}] \le 1/2$ and
$y_i = x_i - \hat\mu_{i-1}$. Since $x_i \in [0,1]$ and $\hat\mu_{i-1} \in (0,1)$ is
$\mathcal F_{i-1}$-measurable, $y_i > -1$; and $\lambda_i \in [0, 3/4] \subset [0,1)$ is
$\mathcal F_{i-1}$-measurable. Fan's inequality states that for all $y \ge -1$ and
$\lambda \in [0,1)$,
$\exp\big(\lambda y - \psi_E(\lambda)\, y^2\big) \le 1 + \lambda y$.
Multiplying both sides by the $\mathcal F_{i-1}$-measurable factor
$\exp\big(\lambda_i(\hat\mu_{i-1} - \tfrac12)\big)$ and using
$\lambda_i(x_i - \tfrac12) = \lambda_i y_i + \lambda_i(\hat\mu_{i-1} - \tfrac12)$,
$$\exp\Big(\lambda_i \big(x_i - \tfrac12\big) - \psi_E(\lambda_i)\, y_i^2\Big) \;\le\; \big(1 + \lambda_i y_i\big)\, e^{\lambda_i (\hat\mu_{i-1} - 1/2)} .$$
Taking $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot \mid \mathcal F_{i-1}]$ of the right-hand side and using
$\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid \mathcal F_{i-1}] = \mu_i - \hat\mu_{i-1}$ together with $1 + u \le e^u$:
$$\big(1 + \lambda_i(\mu_i - \hat\mu_{i-1})\big)\, e^{\lambda_i(\hat\mu_{i-1} - 1/2)} \;\le\; e^{\lambda_i(\mu_i - \hat\mu_{i-1})}\, e^{\lambda_i(\hat\mu_{i-1} - 1/2)} \;=\; e^{\lambda_i(\mu_i - 1/2)} \;\le\; 1,$$
the last step because $\mu_i \le 1/2$ and $\lambda_i \ge 0$. Hence
$\mathbb{E}[W_i \mid \mathcal F_{i-1}] \le W_{i-1}$: $(W_n)$ is a nonnegative supermartingale with
$W_0 = 1$, and Ville's inequality yields $\Pr(\exists n: W_n \ge 1/\alpha) \le \alpha$. $\square$

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Scope.} The argument is the standard testing-by-betting supermartingale bound
\cite{waudbysmith2023betting,howard2021timeuniform}; we claim only the correspondence to this
implementation. Rejecting the weak null establishes that the challenger was conditionally better
at \emph{some} point of the adjudication stream --- not that it is better at commit time, which is
why the cohort and refresh continuation modes of \S S2.13 (relocated from \S\ref{sec:riskgates} of the main paper) exist. The stratified
gates run one such process per class at $\alpha/2$ (or $\alpha/4$ with a futility side) and
Bonferroni preserves the level. A registered null simulation with time-varying conditional means
(all $\le 0$) and time-varying tie probabilities verifies the bound empirically
(\texttt{test\_weak\_null\_drifting\_means} in the artifact).

\section{Total label and compute ledger per policy}

The accounting behind \S\ref{sec:boundaries} of the main paper: candidates dominate every policy's label
bill, the gate's \emph{total} cost exceeds naive's (rejected candidates are trained and
discarded, and rejections keep the detector reference, producing more triggers), and the
probe is about 3\% of the gate's total. This is why ``label-efficient'' in this paper means
the incremental cost of the \emph{decision}, never the cost of the pipeline.

\section{Multiplicity: every family and its adjustment}
\label{sec:s5multiplicity}

The main paper states the policy; this is the table behind it. Families are defined by
evidence tier, not by convenience, and a block is treated as a family only where several
inferential statements are made together.

\textbf{Confirmatory core (Holm).} The six registered gate-versus-naive contrasts --- the
primary $b{=}32$ gate against always-deploying, on the benefit, marginal and harm regimes,
under both the classical and the quantum-kernel detector. Three are nominally significant
(ToN-IoT under both detectors, and CICIDS-PortScan under QK-ZZ) and \emph{all three survive}
Holm step-down control at $\alpha{=}0.05$. The three that do not reach significance are the
benefit- and marginal-regime cells where the paper's claim is \emph{preservation}, not
superiority --- non-inferiority against a pre-registered margin, which is the criterion those
cells were registered under and which the diagnostic table in \S S2.11 reports.

\textbf{Registered follow-ups (Benjamini--Hochberg within block).} The budget frontier
(the fifteen pre-declared cells --- 3 policies $\times$ 5 caps --- on CICIDS-PortScan at
full drift under the Bonferroni schedule, including the two configurations that never
commit) and the chronological matrix (the strict gate on seven pre-enumerated replays) each
form a within-block family fixed in advance of the results. One candid note on design:
the chronological family tests strict against \emph{no-adaptation}; on the
collapsed-incumbent CICIDS replays that contrast is structurally easy to satisfy (any
policy that commits at all clears a collapsed baseline), so BH survival there certifies
little beyond the recovery itself, and the informative gate-versus-always-deploy
comparisons on those streams remain descriptive (main \S5.7). Thirteen of the fifteen
frontier cells and all seven replays survive BH control of the false-discovery rate; the
two non-survivors are exactly the never-committing cells, whose paired gain is identically
zero.

\textbf{Descriptive tier (uncorrected, and labelled).} Ablations, sensitivity sweeps and
auxiliary negative results are reported without correction and without confirmatory language.

\emph{The point of the table is what it does not change.} Every nominally significant contrast
in this paper survives its adjustment, so no conclusion rests on an uncorrected comparison;
the correction is reported because a reader is entitled to check that, not because it rescues
anything. Multiplicity-adjusted $p$-values are computed directly from the paired per-seed
contrasts using a \emph{deterministic centered paired bootstrap test}: with $d$ the seed-level
paired differences (each contrast is a mean over 30 seeds, the unit of inference), the
observed statistic is $|\bar d|$, resampling is performed on $d - \bar d$ (imposing the null),
$B = 100{,}000$, and the two-sided Monte-Carlo--corrected $p$ is
$(\#\{|\bar d^{*}_0| \ge |\bar d|\} + 1)/(B+1)$, with per-contrast RNG seeds derived from the
contrast label (bit-reproducible, order-independent); this is a bootstrap approximation of
the null distribution, not an exact test. Holm controls the six-test confirmatory family, and
Benjamini--Hochberg is applied separately to the pre-declared 15-cell budget-frontier block
(3 policies $\times$ 5 caps on PortScan-full under the Bonferroni schedule, \emph{including}
the two configurations that never commit --- the family is fixed in advance and does not
condition on observed outcomes) and to the seven-replay chronological block. Two pre-declared
sensitivities (paired $t$-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank on $d$) are reported alongside in the
table and agree with the primary analysis; they never replace it. Survival under adjustment:
3 of the 6 core contrasts are nominally significant and all 3 survive Holm; 13 of the 15
frontier cells survive BH (the two non-survivors are exactly the never-committing
configurations, whose paired gain is identically zero); all 7 chronological replays survive
BH. The full machine-readable table is
\path{results/tables/paper2_final_q1/multiplicity.csv} in the artifact.

v1.21.0-code outputs was bit-identical in all five CSVs). At confirmatory scale the

sensitivity $p$-values, in the artifact CSVs; they agree with the primary bootstrap
analysis in every cell). For PortScan, the naive$_{2000}$--never CI90 upper bound is

PERSISTENCE fails (no F1 contrast is $\le -0.5$ pp with CI95 below zero; none is
Holm-significant); ELIMINATION passes its frozen margin criteria (all three F1 contrasts
and all six F3 contrasts CI90-inside $\pm0.5$ pp) but fails the preregistered
harmful-future-value criterion, which keys on the H5 \emph{sign rate} of committed

so the near-50\% sign rates at 2{,}000 are within-trajectory variability, not population
prevalence or deployment probability. The registered classification and margin-based
mean comparison do not demonstrate absence of an effect.

\section{Final exact-cleaned-feature-disjoint integrity sensitivity}
\label{sec:supp_value_disjoint}

\subsection{Forensic audit and role construction}

Exact equality uses the complete cleaned raw feature vector in the experiment's common
feature order after numeric coercion and NaN/infinity handling, represented as canonical
float64 bytes with signed zero normalized. No rounding, scaling, PCA or approximate
matching enters the key. SHA-256 identifies candidate groups and actual vectors are
compared on hash matches; zero collisions were observed. The key is features only, so
the 403 contradictory-label groups in UNSW-NB15 remain intact. Every original row and
label is retained, and within-role multiplicity remains empirical evidence rather than
being deleted.

\input{tables/table_value_disjoint_overlap.tex}

Under the historical source-row splitter, the median scale of overlap is large enough to
matter as an integrity allegation: at seed 6001 the number of exact-$X$ groups spanning
window/train, window/probe, train/probe and all three roles is respectively
20{,}498/15{,}362/11{,}079/6{,}878 for PortScan,
6{,}266/5{,}302/4{,}513/3{,}706 for UNSW-Recon, and
1{,}954/1{,}379/969/430 for ToN-IoT. Across proposals, 5.2--5.9\% of PortScan candidate rows,
10.2--10.7\% of UNSW candidate rows and 8.3--8.5\% of ToN candidate rows have an exact
feature match in later evaluation. Conversely, the share of future evaluation rows with
an exact match in candidate training rises from 1.99\% to 3.18\% (PortScan), 6.81\% to
10.53\% (UNSW), and 7.61\% to 8.10\% (ToN) from 512 to 2{,}000/class. These diagnostics
verify exposure and its size dependence; they do not identify causal bias.

The sensitivity uses deterministic seed-dependent whole-group assignment targeting the
registered 50/30/20 fractions simultaneously in reference/current $\times$ benign/attack
strata. All confirmatory role audits report zero exact-$X$ cross-role overlap, every row
assigned exactly once, multiplicity preserved, contradictory-label groups intact and a
maximum target-fraction deviation of 0.0058 percentage points. Candidate sampling remains
with replacement within the training role and preserves the nested 512 prefix in 2{,}000.

availability was checked from the paper or publisher page in September 2026.}
